title: Calculating tax on stock investment profit
subtitle: Tax implications
openingQuestion: You buy 1,000 VNM shares at VND 60,000/share (VND 60 million total), then sell all of them at VND 75,000/share (VND 75 million total), a gain of VND 15 million. Under Vietnam's current personal income tax rules for listed securities, how must you pay tax?
openingOptions: No tax at all, since this is an officially listed stock
20% on the VND 15 million gain, as US capital gains tax works
Pay 0.1% of the sale value: 0.1% × 75 million = VND 75,000
0.1% but only on the VND 15 million gain, not the sale value
explanation: Under current Vietnamese personal income tax rules, an individual investor pays 0.1% tax on the TOTAL SALE VALUE of each securities transfer, regardless of gain or loss, and not calculated as a percentage of profit the way US-style capital gains tax works. This tax is usually automatically withheld by the securities company right when the sell order matches.

realWorldExample.company: Automatic tax withholding through securities companies (SSI, VNDirect, VPS...)
realWorldExample.description: When an investor places a sell order through a securities company like SSI, VNDirect or VPS, the system automatically withholds 0.1% personal income tax on the sale value the moment the order matches, plus the securities company's trading fee (usually 0.1%-0.25% depending on company and service tier). The investor receives the sale proceeds already net of tax and fees, with no need to separately declare or pay this tax.

quiz.question: How is personal income tax on transferring listed securities in Vietnam calculated?
options: 0.1% on the sale value each time, regardless of gain or loss
20% on the profit, similar to capital gains tax in the US, a rule many newcomers get wrong at first
Fully exempt for already-listed securities
10% on the total sale value of each transaction
quiz.explanation: Vietnam applies a flat 0.1% tax on the sale value (sale revenue), not on profit. This is fundamentally different from capital gains tax in the US, where tax only applies to the gain portion.

quiz.question: If an investor sells a stock at a LOSS (sale price lower than purchase price), do they still have to pay the 0.1% personal income tax?
options: No, a losing trade doesn't create a tax obligation
Yes, because the tax is calculated on sale value, not on profit
Only if the loss exceeds 10% of the purchase price
The tax already paid is refunded once the loss is confirmed
quiz.explanation: This is the most important difference from US-style capital gains tax: because the 0.1% tax is calculated on sale value (not profit), the investor still has to pay this tax even when selling at a loss.

quiz.question: How is a cash dividend received from a listed stock taxed under personal income tax?
options: Taxed at 0.1%, the same as when selling stock on the exchange
Taxed at 20%, like the company's corporate income tax
Not subject to personal income tax when receiving a dividend
Taxed at 5%, withheld at source before payment
quiz.explanation: Cash dividends to individuals are subject to personal income tax on investment income at a 5% rate on the total dividend amount, withheld at source. This is a separate tax from the 0.1% tax on selling securities.

quiz.question: An investor sells a block of stock worth VND 200 million, of which the original cost was VND 180 million. What personal income tax must be paid?
options: VND 1 million (= VND 20 million gain × 5%, the same rate as the dividend tax)
VND 20,000 (= VND 20 million gain × 0.1%)
VND 4 million (= VND 20 million gain × 20%)
VND 200,000, calculated on the total sale value of VND 200 million
quiz.explanation: Tax is calculated on total transfer value, not on profit: 200 million × 0.1% = VND 200,000. All other options apply a capital-gains or investment-income tax calculation method, not the current rule for listed securities.

quiz.question: Why does the 0.1%-of-sale-value method make excessively frequent trading more costly than most people realize?
options: Because it's collected every time you sell, so the tax accumulates with each round-trip in a year
Because the tax rate keeps increasing with the number of trades an investor makes, a cost easy to underestimate at a glance
Because the tax from losing trades gets added onto the next winning trade
Because the investor must personally re-finalize all transactions at year-end
quiz.explanation: The tax is collected on every sale, so turning over your portfolio ten times a year means paying it ten times on the full value each time - plus the trading fee on both the buy and the sell order. This cost doesn't show up as a single number, so it's very easy to overlook when calculating overall efficiency.

keyTakeaways: Personal income tax on selling listed securities in Vietnam is 0.1% on the TOTAL SALE VALUE of each transaction, not on the profit portion like US-style capital gains tax
This 0.1% tax applies regardless of whether the transaction is a gain or a loss, and is usually automatically withheld by the securities company right when the sell order matches
Cash dividends are subject to a separate personal income tax of 5% on the amount received, withheld at source
Because the tax is calculated on sale value rather than profit, the more frequently you trade (buying and selling repeatedly), the more the total tax owed accumulates, regardless of gain or loss

practicePrompt.question: You buy 2,000 shares at VND 30,000 (VND 60 million total), then sell at VND 25,000 (VND 50 million total) - a loss of VND 10 million. Do you have to pay personal income tax on this transaction?
options: Yes, still pay 0.1% on the sale value (VND 50,000), since the tax is calculated on sale revenue
No, because this transaction is a loss so it doesn't trigger any personal income tax obligation at all
Yes, but only pay tax calculated on the VND 10 million loss using the same 0.1% formula
Can't be determined without knowing exactly how long the stock was held before selling
practicePrompt.explanation: The 0.1% personal income tax is calculated on total sale value (VND 50 million), not on profit, so it must still be paid even though this transaction was a loss.

sections.text: Many people learning to invest in Vietnam, when reading English-language material about the US's 'capital gains tax', easily misunderstand that Vietnam calculates tax the same way - on the profit. In reality, Vietnam's securities tax mechanism is quite different.
A 0.1% tax on sale value, not on profit

Under current personal income tax rules, when an individual transfers (sells) securities listed on HOSE, HNX or UPCoM, personal income tax is calculated as 0.1% of the TOTAL SALE VALUE of that transaction - not on the gain between sale price and purchase price. This is a fundamental difference from capital gains tax in the US, where tax is only levied on the actual profit portion and the rate varies by holding period.

A concrete example: you sell 1,000 shares at VND 75,000/share, for a total sale value of VND 75 million. The personal income tax owed is 75,000,000 x 0.1% = VND 75,000 - regardless of the price you originally bought at, and regardless of whether this transaction is a gain or a loss.

sections.label: Why you still pay tax even when selling at a loss
sections.text: Because the 0.1% tax is calculated on sale revenue rather than profit, an investor who sells stock at a price lower than the purchase price (a loss) still has to pay the full 0.1% on that sale value. This surprises many people, since intuition usually says 'no profit, no tax' - but Vietnam's flat-rate tax mechanism doesn't work on that logic.

Besides the tax on selling, cash dividends an individual investor receives from a stock are also subject to a separate personal income tax, at a 5% rate on the total dividend amount received. This tax is usually withheld at source by the company or the depository before payment, so the investor receives the amount already net of tax.

items: Tax on selling listed securities: 0.1% on total sale value each transaction, regardless of gain/loss
Tax on cash dividends: 5% on the dividend amount received, withheld at source
Stock dividends or bonus shares: no tax due immediately upon receipt, tax is calculated when those shares are later sold (at the 0.1% rate on sale value)
The 0.1% tax is usually automatically withheld by the securities company right when the sell order matches, no separate declaration needed

sections.text: Because the tax is calculated on sale value rather than profit, the actual tax cost is essentially proportional to TRADING FREQUENCY, not to the level of gain. This is one more reason (alongside trading fees) why excessively frequent trading (overtrading, mentioned in the previous lesson) erodes net profit more than investors think.

lines: Vietnam's stock tax is 0.1% on the sale value of each transaction - not on profit, and it applies even when selling at a loss.
Understanding the tax mechanism correctly helps you calculate your true net return accurately, instead of confusing it with the US-style capital gains tax calculation.
